title: Fit a wrench, release a captive latch nut and open its arm
instruction: Release the captive nut that clamps the swing arm, using the wrenches on the rack, and open the arm to its stop without rounding the nut. At the end every wrench must be back in its own place on the rack, and nothing may touch the nut, the arm or any wrench for 20 seconds.
context: Industrial machinery mechanics and maintenance workers loosen fasteners with hand wrenches as routine work, and must choose a close metric/imperial fit before applying torque: a wrong fit can permanently round a captive nut before its clamp is released. Here the nut is unmarked and the five open-end wrenches on the rack differ by only 0.3 to 1.3 mm in jaw opening. Which one fits is not stated; a trial fit shows it: the 12 mm does not go on, the 13 mm, 14 mm and adjustable go on with play and round the nut under load, and only the 1/2 in turns it. Afterwards the tools go back on the rack. Unlike fixed-wrench pipe-union or ratchet-direction tasks, this combines unmarked tool-fit selection, clearance-sensitive damage, returning the tools and hands-off proof after opening a released arm.
setup: Coordinates in metres, x forward, y left, z up. Standard station: table top at z 0.7475, standard cameras, both YAM arms at their standard bases (0, +0.305, 0.75) and (0, -0.305, 0.75), both in the ready pose with grippers open. Latch fixture, fixed to the table: a steel pillar 22 x 22 x 84 mm at (0.28, 0.12); on it a captive steel hex nut, 12.70 mm across flats (1/2 in), 6.8 mm tall, unmarked, with a yellow paint mark, bearing face at z 0.8375; a steel swing arm (bar 18 x 98 x 4.4 mm, 0.09 kg, black knob 12 mm in diameter and 36 mm tall at 80 mm from the pivot) on a vertical pivot on the nut's axis at z 0.833. The arm starts pointing toward -y; its open stop is 90 degrees away, pointing toward -x. The arm is clamped until the nut has been turned more than 60 degrees counter-clockwise (seen from above); the nut needs 0.35 N m to break free and 0.03 N m after 2 degrees. Tool rack: ten fixed steel blocks 16 x 32 x 35 mm, two per wrench, 155 mm apart along x. Five free steel open-end wrenches, 5 mm thick, lie flat across their two blocks with handles pointing +x and jaw centres at (0.30, y, 0.785), y = 0.50, 0.45, 0.40, 0.35, 0.30: 12 mm (jaw opening 12.05 mm), 1/2 in (12.75 mm), 13 mm (13.05 mm) and 14 mm (14.05 mm), each 160 mm from jaw centre to handle end and 0.11 kg; and an adjustable wrench preset to 13.55 mm, 200 mm, 0.24 kg (its worm screw does not turn). Under load: the 1/2 in turns the nut without damage; a wrench with more clearance rounds the nut once the turning torque stays above 0.20 N m (13 mm), 0.14 N m (adjustable) or 0.08 N m (14 mm) for 10 ms; the 12 mm does not go on and rounds the nut if forced with more than 0.05 N m. A rounded nut turns bright and spins on its stud, and the clamp then never lets go. Friction: wrenches 0.2, rack blocks 1.0. Arms: total joint torque including gravity 27 N m (joints 1 to 3) and 7 N m (joints 4 to 6), 40 N per finger. Physics at 2 ms (25 steps per action). Fixed layout, no jitter (object_jitter=0).
scoring: Scored on the state at the end of the episode; everything can be checked with a protractor, a ruler and the video. The nut is released when its paint mark has turned more than 60 degrees counter-clockwise from its start and it is not rounded (a rounded nut shows bright corners and spins freely). Hands off means no part of either robot and no wrench touches the nut or the arm. A wrench is back in its rack position when it lies flat on its own two rack blocks: its jaw centre within 10 mm horizontally of its marked rack position and within 3 mm of its rack height, its long axis within 10 degrees of the rack direction (handle toward +x), its face within 5 degrees of horizontal (either face up), and no part of either robot touches any wrench. 1.0: nut released, hands off, arm open at least 85 degrees (the stop is at 90) and all five wrenches back in their own rack positions, all continuously for 20 s; the episode then ends with success. 0.5: nut released and hands off continuously for the last 20 s of the episode, with the arm at any angle or a wrench not back in its rack position (for example the used wrench left on the table). 0 otherwise. A rounded nut can never count as released, so rounding scores 0 for the rest of the episode. A state that cannot be read scores 0. The simulator checks these every 2 ms physics step; any break restarts the 20 s count.
reset_notes: Reset restores the fixed layout: all five wrenches on the rack, the nut unturned and not rounded, the arm clamped shut, both robots in the ready pose. For a real trial, replace a rounded nut. The Inspect seed does not change the scene.
fidelity: Rigid parts, CPU physics at 2 ms. Nut and wrench sizes and clearances are real, but torques are scaled down: the nut breaks free at 0.35 N m, where a real nut of this size is tightened to roughly 10 to 25 N m, because the arms' wrist joints give only 7 N m. No thread is simulated: the clamp lets go at a 60 degree turn, and rounding is an event (a loose fit under torque above a threshold for 10 ms) that leaves the nut spinning. The adjustable wrench's worm is not modelled.
